top_organisms.name: Streptococcus mitis
top_organisms.significance: It is an early coloniser of oral cavity and colonises infant’s oral cavity soon after birth. It is a commensal bacterium and one of the dominant species in children up to the age of 4 years. It produces hydrogen peroxide which prevents colonisation of harmful pathogens

top_organisms.name: Veillonella parvula
top_organisms.significance: V. parvula is a gram-negative coccus which exists as a member of the oral microbiome. This organism can lead to periodontist and different systemic infections. Introductory studies conducted on role of this bacterium in human health pointed towards its increased abundance in patients suffering from pancreatic ductal carcinoma

top_organisms.name: Rothia SGB49305
top_organisms.significance: Rothia is a gram-positive and commensal bacteria. It helps in nitric oxide and gluten degradation. Some species may associate with oral infection

top_organisms.name: Actinomyces johnsonii
top_organisms.significance: Actinomyces johnsonii is a common oral commensal, often found in dental plaque and healthy gingival tissues. It has been linked to recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS), showing increased abundance and cytotoxic effects on oral epithelial cells

top_organisms.name: Actinomyces massiliensis
top_organisms.significance: The Actinomyces spp. are found to be abundant in healthy individuals. Decreased abundance is associated with various oral diseases. Although Actinomyces spp. are responsible for production of biofilm on tooth surfaces, however, they are not associated with periodontitis

top_organisms.name: Corynebacterium matruchotii
top_organisms.significance: Corynebacterium matruchotii is an actinobacteria commonly occurring as a part of core microflora of the tooth. Presence of this bacterium in oral cavity is an indicator of caries free tooth. Its reduced / lower abundance reflects a shift to caries biofilm from a healthy dental plaque. Abundance of the bacteria is inversely proportional to cancer risk in head and neck squamous cells as well as reduced smoking

top_organisms.name: Actinomyces dentalis
top_organisms.significance: Actinomyces dentalis is a Gram-positive bacterium first isolated from a human dental abscess, indicating its role in oral infections. It may contribute to pus formation and tissue damage, but its specific functions in the oral microbiome are not well-characterized

top_organisms.name: Streptococcus oralis
top_organisms.significance: It is an early coloniser found in dental plaques. It produces hydrogen peroxide which prevents the pathogenic bacteria from commencing disease

top_organisms.name: GGB1844 SGB2532
top_organisms.significance: The unclassified species taxonomy belongs to Porphyromonadaceae family of Gram-negative bacteria, of the order Bacteroidales. Members of this family reside in the human oral cavity as commensals or as opportunistic pathogens

top_organisms.name: Gemella haemolysans
top_organisms.significance: It colonises the mucous membranes of the oral cavity. This gram- positive facultative anaerobes ferments frees sugars and produces a mixture of acid end products together with carbon dioxide

top_organisms.name: Streptococcus sanguinis
top_organisms.significance: This early coloniser delays colonisation of Streptococcus mutans (responsible for tooth decay), resulting in decreased caries in primary and permanent teeth

top_organisms.name: Streptococcus parasanguinis
top_organisms.significance: It is pioneer coloniser and arginolyitc bacteria, capable of preventing growth of aciduric bacteria. It delays colonisation of Streptococcus mutans, hence, preventing caries formation in primary and permanent teeth

top_organisms.name: Streptococcus gordonii
top_organisms.significance: Salivary amylase produces by host aids in colonisation of S. gordonii in the oral cavity of children. Establishment of this bacterium is crucial for establishment of late colonisers in mouth. Presence of this bacterium is linked to reduced prevalence of Streptocccus mutans and dental caries

top_organisms.name: Veillonella atypica
top_organisms.significance: Veillonella rogosae is a gram-negative anaerobic bacterium that plays a role in early dental biofilm formation by metabolizing lactate produced by other bacteria. It contributes to oral microbial balance and may help reduce the risk of dental caries by lowering acid levels

top_organisms.name: Streptococcus salivarius
top_organisms.significance: This bacterium is abundant in saliva and oropharyngeal mucosa of the oral cavity. Salivary amylase produces by host aids in colonisation of S. salivarius in the oral cavity of children. Establishment of this bacterium is crucial for establishment of late colonisers in mouth. It possesses anti-inflammatory properties

top_organisms.name: Veillonella rogosae
top_organisms.significance: It converts lactic acid to weak acids like formic acid, acetic acid and propionic acid. These weak acids help in acid neutralization and tooth re-mineralisation by interfering with Streptococcus mutans. It interacts positively with Streptococcus australis while interfering with cariogenic bacteria

What is the oral microbiome, and why is it important for your health?
The oral cavity harbours a complex and diverse community of microorganisms, collectively forming the oral
microbiome. This intricate network profoundly influences various aspects of our lives, starting from the moment
of birth when the assembly of this microbiome begins. Throughout our lives, these oral microbes play crucial
roles in processes such as digestion and the synthesis of essential compounds that contribute to nutrient
absorption.
The oral microbiome's impact extends deeply into our overall health, intricately shaping the health of our teeth,
gums, and even influencing our systemic well-being. From breaking down food particles during the initial stages
of digestion to actively participating in immune system education, the oral microbiome contributes significantly
to our health.
Analyzing the oral microbiome involves studying the genes of various microorganisms, including bacteria,
viruses, fungi, and other microbes present in the oral cavity. This comprehensive examination generates a
detailed report outlining the microbial composition within the oral environment. Beyond identification, this
analysis can detect genes related to antibiotic resistance, aiding healthcare professionals in determining effective
treatment options for oral infections.
The report not only lists the types of microbes but also provides detailed information about potentially harmful
ones, offering insights into their identity and genetic traits. This information is valuable for understanding the
diverse range of microbes residing in the oral cavity and their implications for oral health. Furthermore,
maintaining a balanced oral microbiome is essential for preventing issues such as tooth decay, gum disease, and
other oral health conditions. Adopting good oral hygiene practices and making lifestyle choices that support a
healthy oral microbiome contribute to overall oral and systemic well-being.

Condition-specific microbial markers
What is a biomarker?
The FDA defines a biomarker as a measurable characteristic to tell how the body is doing and overall health. It is
a measurable indicator or characteristic that can be objectively assessed and used as a signpost for biological
processes, conditions, or diseases in the body. In the context of the oral microbiome analysis, Microbial markers
are specific molecules, genes, or organisms found in the microbiome that can signal various aspects of oral health,
disease risk, or treatment response.
Microbial markers in oral microbiome analysis serve several important purposes:
 Health Assessment: Help assess the overall health status of the oral cavity. For example, the presence or
absence of certain bacteria or microbial by-products can indicate whether the oral environment is healthy
or potentially associated with disease.
 Disease Identification: Specific microbial markers may be linked to particular oral diseases or conditions.
Changes in the abundance or diversity of certain microbial species could signal conditions such as
periodontal disease, gingivitis, or dental caries.
 Treatment Efficacy: Can be used to evaluate how the oral microbiome responds to various treatments or
interventions. Monitoring changes in these markers helps assess the effectiveness of therapeutic
approaches.
 Predictive Indicators: Serve as predictive markers, offering insights into an individual's susceptibility
to certain oral diseases or their potential response to specific treatments based on their unique oral
microbiome profile.
Identifying and understanding these microbial markers in the oral microbiome provides valuable insights into
oral health, disease mechanisms, and personalized approaches for improving oral conditions.

Overall lifestyle recommendations
Maintaining a healthy oral microbiome is essential for overall oral health. Here are lifestyle recommendations to
promote a healthy oral microbiome and limit dysbiosis:
 Practice Good Oral Hygiene: Brush your teeth twice a day using fluoride toothpaste. Floss daily to
remove plaque and debris from between teeth.
Client Name: Collection Date: Version 2 7 | Pa ge
 Use Antimicrobial Mouthwash Sparingly: While mouthwash can help kill bacteria, excessive use may
disrupt the natural balance of the oral microbiome. Use antimicrobial mouthwash as directed or as
recommended by your dentist.
 Consume a Balanced Diet: Eat a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins.
 Limit sugary and acidic foods, as they can contribute to the growth of harmful bacteria.
 Stay Hydrated: Drinking water helps flush away food particles and bacteria, promoting a healthier oral
environment.
 Chew Sugar-Free Gum: This can stimulate saliva production, which helps neutralize acids and
maintain a balanced pH in the mouth.
 Quit Smoking and Tobacco Products: Smoking and tobacco use can contribute to gum disease and
negatively impact the oral microbiome.
 Eliminate Alcohol Consumption: Excessive alcohol consumption can contribute to dry mouth,
reducing saliva production.
 Regular Dental Check-ups: Visit your dentist for regular check-ups and cleanings.
 Manage Stress: Practice stress-reducing techniques such as meditation, deep breathing, or yoga.
 Limit Antibiotic Use: Only take antibiotics as prescribed by a healthcare professional and complete the
full course.
 Address Teeth Grinding (Bruxism): If you grind your teeth, discuss potential solutions with your
dentist, as bruxism can contribute to oral health issues.
By embracing these simple yet effective lifestyle adjustments, you can cultivate an environment in your oral
cavity that encourages the growth of beneficial bacteria, ultimately supporting a healthier microbiome and
overall well-being.

Appendix
What is the technology employed by BioAro?
The human body contains trillions of microorganisms. These microorganisms have been known to impact host health in various ways.
Knowing what microbes are present helps us to understand how our body responds to dietary interventions, drugs, or food choices and
how we can manipulate them to receive maximum health benefits.
We, at BioAro, care for your health therefore, we try to target every microbe in your sample! How do we ensure that? We
perform comprehensive microbiome analysis by employing state of art technology such as shotgun sequencing, which enables detection
of all kinds of microbes including bacteria, fungi, viruses, and other types of eukaryotes. Not only this, but the approach also performs
better taxonomic resolution and coverage, while simultaneously giving information about the functional microbiome profile.
Glossary of important terms and definitions:
Alpha-diversity (Shannon Index) helps us determine the diversity of species within an ecosystem. In simple words, it answers the
question of ‘How Many?’. Alpha diversity can be explained by describing:
· Species richness: This provides a count of the number of different species present in a sample. It does not consider the abundance of
the species or their relative distributions.
· Species evenness: This is a measure of relative abundance of different species present in a sample.
High diversity value of plague profile indicates that the microbiome comprises of variety of microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, viruses,
archaea) that can produce variety a wide range of metabolites and can positively affect the resilience and stability of the plague
microbiome in times of dysbiosis and stress. Loss of microbiome diversity (LOMD) is described to be one of the most constant factors
while studying dysbiosis or imbalance.
Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes are two most important groups of bacteria of the human plague microbiome. The proportion of
Firmicutes found in the plague, affecting your F/B ratio, is implicated in many health conditions. Larger amount of Firmicutes in
comparison to Bacteroidetes is often found in obese people. There are different species in each group with varied abilities. Usually fat-
rich diet is known to increase the firmicutes in your plaque and fiber-rich diet could increase the beneficial species of Bacteroidetes.
Dysbiosis: It refers to disruption of the normal microbiome which causes a change in the functional/metabolic composition of the host
microbiome leading to overgrowth of organisms that are otherwise underrepresented or absent in healthy systems.
Keystone Species: Keystone species is one which defines the whole ecosystem owing to its direct effect on the functional role of other
species irrespective of its relative biomass in comparison to the rest of the species.
Simply put, the presence of these species, largely affects the presence/absence of other organisms in the ecosystem and therefore, it is
one of the most crucial members of the ecosystem.
Short Chain Fatty Acids (SCFA): These comprise as one of the main metabolites produced by fermentation of dietary fibers by the
plague microbiota which provide immense health benefits to the host.
